hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when something big is about to start, what do you do first?
options: that’s a beginning before the beginning. hold onto it. listen.
then you already know part of this story. listen.
fair. stay with me, this one starts with a very sudden beginning.

steps.line: Near Mecca, high on a bare mountain, is a small cave called Hira. Before his calling, Muhammad ﷺ often went there alone to pray.
Then, in the cave, the angel Jibril came to him with one word: “Read!”

steps.q: He is told, “Read!” He has never learned to read. What do you think he answers?
o: Nothing. He runs out of the cave.
steps.why: “I am not a reader,” he said. Three times the command came, and three times he said it.

steps.line: “I am not a reader,” he said. Three times the command came. Then the first words: “Read in the name of your Lord, who created.”

steps.q: Iqra, “read!”, shares its root with the name of the book itself. What does Qur’an mean?
steps.why: Qur’an comes from the same root as iqra: read aloud, recite. The book is named for that first command, and it is still learned by reciting aloud.

steps.line: He hurried home, shaking, and said to his wife Khadijah, “Cover me, cover me.” She wrapped him up and stayed beside him.
“God will never disgrace you,” she told him. “You are good to your family, you carry the weak, you welcome guests.” She stood by him from the very start.

steps.q: Why might the first verse say “read in the name of your Lord,” and not simply “read”?
o: To show reading is only for prayer
So he would not be starting alone
To give the book its title
steps.why: Starting in God’s name means the work isn’t done alone. In Muslim teaching, the beginning is carried.

steps.line: Today, many Muslims say “bismillah,” in the name of God, before a meal, a drive, an exam. Nothing starts alone.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Bismillah opens almost every chapter of the Qur’an. How many of its 114?
steps.why: All but the ninth open with it, and it also appears inside the twenty-seventh, in a letter from Solomon. So it’s there 114 times after all.

say: here’s what i love. the very first word was “read,” and right behind it came “in the name of your Lord.”
that’s the spirit of bismillah. in islam, you don’t begin alone. even the smallest start, a bite of food, is begun in God’s name.

steps.q: He said three times that he couldn’t read, and the command still came. What does that suggest about beginnings?
o: You can start before you feel ready
Only the ready ones get called
Repeating a thing makes it come true
steps.why: He didn’t feel ready, and he began anyway, in God’s name. That’s the heart of bismillah: you never begin alone.

today.say: before the next thing you start today, a meal, a message, the car, say “bismillah,” out loud or under your breath. or just give it one full pause.
options: lovely. that one small word starts so many beginnings, every single day.
that counts. the pause is where the name goes.

card.keepWhy: Read, in the name of your Lord. Nothing starts alone.
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3 (the beginning of revelation in the cave of Hira: “Read!”, “I am not a reader”, the three embraces, “cover me”, Khadijah’s reassurance)
Qur’an 96:1–5 (“Read in the name of your Lord who created … who taught by the pen”), paraphrased
Sahih al-Bukhari 5376; Sahih Muslim 2022 (say bismillah before eating)
check: Khadijah’s words are paraphrased and shortened from Bukhari 3 (she lists more: speaking the truth, helping those in hardship). Confirm the shortening.

Linking the first revelation’s “in the name of your Lord” (iqra’ bismi rabbik) to the everyday bismillah is a teaching link (the lesson says “the spirit of bismillah”), not a claim that one comes from the other. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable with it.
